title: Why advisor marketing belongs in the C-suite
hook: Your recruiting promise shows up in an advisor’s everyday experience.
script:
If you lead a wealth management firm, your recruiting story probably talks about support. Here’s the question I would ask next: what does that support look like on an ordinary Tuesday?

Can an advisor explain who they serve? Do they know where to go when their website needs work? Is there a clear way to get a useful piece of content from an idea through review?

That is why I see advisor marketing as a leadership responsibility.

In my fractional CMO work, I connect the firm’s brand strategy, the marketing team, the recruiting priorities, and the work advisors actually need. Those decisions belong in the same conversation.

A useful starting exercise is to put your recruiting promise on one side of a page and the actual advisor experience on the other. Pick one promise. Follow it through. Who owns it? What happens? Where does it get stuck?

That gives you something concrete to improve and something the team can own.

If you lead a firm, which part of that connection is hardest to make today?
shots: Open seated at the desk, speaking to a firm leader; hold a sheet with “Promise” and “Experience.”
Cut to a clean, fictional two-column worksheet. Write “Marketing support” and “Who owns the next step?”
Return to camera for the CMO role and final question. Keep the close conversational.
overlays: Brand strategy · Team leadership · Advisor support
caption: Your recruiting story makes a promise. Your advisor experience shows how that promise works. In my fractional CMO work, I connect the firm’s brand, marketing team, recruiting priorities, and advisor support. A useful exercise: choose one promise and follow it through to the person responsible for delivering it. Where does that connection get difficult in your firm?
companion: Firm leader worksheet: list one recruiting promise, the advisor action it should enable, the responsible person, the current process, and one gap to fix. Label it a proposed exercise, not a Coastal Wealth document.
cta: Ask a firm-level question in the post. Profile and website point to For firms.
proof: Role and scope come from Keir’s account. No recruiting result, adoption rate, or client statement is claimed.

title: Who should recognize themselves in your first sentence?
hook: Read your first sentence and ask: who knows this is for them?
script:
Here’s a quick way to check your advisor website. Read only the first sentence. Can a person you want to work with recognize their situation?

“Helping individuals and families pursue their financial goals” describes a lot of practices. It leaves your visitor to work out whether you understand them.

Try starting with a real situation instead. Here’s a fictional example: “I help business owners organize the personal financial decisions around a possible sale.”

That sentence still needs support. What work do you actually do? What experience can you explain? How can you reach those people? A sharper sentence is a direction to test, not proof you’ve found your market.

I help advisors work through those questions inside firms, and I’ve made a quick-start client brief available on my site. It walks through the client, the situation, your approach, and the evidence behind it.

Use it to draft a clearer introduction. Then ask someone you want to serve what they think it means.

For firm leaders, this is also a useful question: how consistently are we helping our advisors do this work?
shots: Open on camera with a printed fictional headline. Circle “individuals and families.”
Show the client-brief tool using its fictional example; avoid personal or client information.
Write the specific introduction on paper, then return to camera for the firm-level bridge.
caption: Your first sentence should help the intended client recognize their situation. Start with a person, a moment, and the help you actually provide. The quick-start Positioning Blueprint on my site can help you draft and test that introduction. Firm leaders: is there a repeatable way your advisors get this support?
companion: A short carousel: broad statement; fictional situation-specific statement; the three questions behind it; a link to the client brief. Use the example label on every slide containing the fictional advisor.
cta: Point to /tools/client-brief/. The firm bridge is a closing observation, not a second sales pitch.
proof: This is a teaching example. Do not present it as a before-and-after client result.

title: What does a referral find before they call?
hook: A warm introduction still sends someone to your website.
script:
Someone recommends you to a friend. Before that person reaches out, they may search your name, visit your website, or look at your profile.

What would they understand without you in the room?

I would check three things. Can they see the client situation you work with? Do your website and profile explain the same kind of help? Can they understand what happens if they contact you?

You don’t need to rewrite everything at once. Put your introduction and your homepage side by side. Find the point where they stop telling the same story. That is a useful place to start.

The Sniff Test on my site helps you review those questions yourself. It organizes your answers into priorities. It doesn’t crawl the internet or predict how many clients you’ll get.

This is the kind of small, practical improvement I like helping advisors make.

And from the firm’s perspective, there’s a bigger opportunity: make this a repeatable part of advisor support, with someone responsible for helping the advisor follow through.

What would a referred prospect still have to ask you after reading your website?
shots: Open with “A friend gave me your name” written on a note. No fabricated incoming message screenshot.
Use a clearly fictional profile and headline, then show the live self-review tool.
End on camera and pause after the question.
overlays: What do they understand without you?
caption: A referral gives someone a reason to look. Your presence should help them understand what they find. Compare your introduction, homepage, and next step. Fix one inconsistency. The Sniff Test is available on my site if you want a structured starting point.
companion: Publish the complete referral-presence guide and a single-page self-review exercise. Link the post directly to the guide or tool, using one destination per post.
cta: Point to /tools/presence-check/. Invite a useful question; do not request private client information.
proof: No traffic-to-inquiry claim. The tool is a self-review, not an automated audit.

title: Before another AI tool, map the handoff
hook: Before you choose another AI tool, choose the workflow you want to improve.
script:
Before adding another AI tool to a marketing team, I want to understand one workflow.

Take turning an advisor conversation into useful content. Where does the source material come from? Who checks that the draft is accurate? Who reviews it for the firm? Who publishes it?

If those responsibilities are unclear, the tool doesn’t resolve them.

Here’s the approach I would use. Map the current steps. Pick one bounded task, such as organizing an interview into a draft brief. Define what a good output looks like. Keep a named person responsible for checking it. Then compare the pilot with the current process.

Look at preparation time, the amount of rework, and whether the final material actually gets used. Use only information and tools the firm permits.

That is the connection I care about between marketing leadership and AI: a better way of getting useful work through the team.

This is an example of the method, not a claim of a measured client deployment.

If you lead a marketing team, which handoff would you improve first?
shots: Open at a whiteboard headed “One workflow.”
Draw four named steps: advisor conversation, draft brief, human/firm review, publish. Write an owner under each.
Close seated. Film a clean board insert for a companion post.
overlays: Pilot task: organize an interview into a draft brief
caption: Practical AI starts with a workflow and a person responsible for the result. For an advisor-content pilot, I would map the source, drafting, review, and publishing steps before choosing the tool. Then compare preparation time, rework, and actual use. This is a proposed method, not a reported client result. Which handoff would you improve first?
companion: A workflow sheet with current steps, proposed bounded task, permitted inputs, reviewer, baseline definition, pilot measure, and decision date. Do not add invented time-saved figures.
cta: Ask a workflow question. Firm leaders can explore the CMO role from the profile.
proof: Keep method language conditional. Do not imply AI was deployed at Coastal Wealth or claim measured savings without evidence.

title: One client question can give you a useful content starting point
hook: You don’t have to start a content plan with a blank calendar.
script:
If you keep getting stuck on content, start with a question you have already heard from the people you want to serve.

Let’s use a simple one: “What happens in a first planning conversation?”

You can answer that directly. You can explain what someone might prepare. You can clear up a common misunderstanding. And you can show the steps in your process.

Those are four angles on one useful question. They only work if they describe what your practice actually does and go through your normal review process.

The client-question planner on my site turns your starting answer into four outlines. You still supply the experience, examples, and judgment that make the content yours.

I share this because helping advisors communicate is part of my fractional CMO work. At the firm level, the next questions are about delivery: where do these questions get captured, who helps shape the drafts, and how does the work move through review?

For your own practice, start smaller. Choose one real question and record a clear answer.

What do prospective clients ask you before that first conversation?
shots: Open with a blank calendar, then move it aside and hold a card with the question.
Screen-record the planner with the fictional example and show the four headings, not a wall of text.
Record the four angles as quick separate lines, then the final question to camera.
overlays: Start with a question you have heard
Answer · Prepare · Clarify · Show the process
caption: Start with a real client question. Answer it, help someone prepare, clarify a misunderstanding, and show your process. The client-question planner can help organize those four angles. Supply your own factual examples and use your firm’s normal review process. What question could you answer this week?
companion: Share the four-week outlines as a fictional sample and link to /tools/content-plan/. Create one short follow-up post about the firm workflow behind advisor content.
cta: Point to /tools/content-plan/. Invite the question, not client names or personal financial details.
proof: No claim that this schedule creates leads. The tool produces outlines and needs human input.
